articles.title: Hopkins Sports in Review (Nov. 9 - 15): Hockey and soccer keep on rolling!
articles.description: The season is coming to a close, and as such we've officially reached the NCAA playoffs! Hopkins has had some strong performances across the last few years, and the hope is that we can win some championships in a push for this year's Learfield Directors' Cup. With that being said, let's take a look back at some of the best performances from the Blue Jays from this past week. Field Hockey: W (2 - 0), W (1 - 0), W (2 - 1 2OT) In what has been an incredibly successful season for the Women's Field Hockey team, the Blue Jays travelled to the NCAA tournament fresh off a Centennial Conference Championship. Their first matchup was against unranked Denison University at Homewood Field. Hopkins registered the first score of the match in the first period thanks to a penalty shot from sophomore midfielder Sarah Chilton. Their second score came in the third quarter from sophomore midfielder Catherine D'Arcy, cementing a dominant win for the home side. Next up were seventh-ranked Stevenson University in a match that took place in Medford, Massachusetts. It was never going to be an easy contest for the Blue Jays, but a gritty display of defense in the first quarter helped them stay competitive. Junior goalie Jessica Lapidus was responsible for four saves that enabled Hopkins to keep it a level scoreline heading into the second period. Smelling blood, the Blue Jays managed to score with four minutes left in the first half in what ended up being the deciding moment of the game. The tuff-est matchup of the week came in their quarterfinal game against Tufts University, the top ranked team in the nation. Hopkins got off to a great start, with sophomore forward Evie Hamm scoring the opening goal of the contest in the first quarter. Tufts managed a response in the second period, tying the game up at one a piece. Some brilliant goalkeeping from Lapidus allowed Hopkins to survive regulation without conceding another goal, at which point it was anyone's game. The first period of overtime saw Tufts take eight shots to Hopkins' three, but none of them managed to find the back of the net. It was a 73rd minute shot from senior forward Sophia Albano that broke the tie and hand Hopkins a victory in a major upset. The team will travel to Geneva, NY this Friday to take on third ranked Christopher Newport in the NCAA semifinal! Football: W (17 - 3) With this being the final game of a disappointing regular season, the odds were not in favor of Hopkins coming out on top of a strong Franklin & Marshall team. Nevertheless, the game is won on the field, not on paper, and Hopkins hoped to put up a tough performance against their conference rivals. The Diplomats received the ball first, but the drive ended quickly with a punt back to the Blue Jays, a good start! Unfortunately, Hopkins could not make much out of their opening possessions either as the ball flipped between the teams. Franklin & Marshall kicked a field goal at the end of the first quarter, but there was not a substantial difference separating the two teams. However, once the second quarter came around, the Blue Jays were able to establish some rhythm on offense, leading a five minute 70-yard drive that resulted in a touchdown. They ended the quarter with a field goal, pushing the margin to seven at the half. A couple of empty possessions to begin the half were quickly forgotten after a quick two-minute drive capped off by a 28-yard receiving touchdown to sophomore wide receiver Alex Orecchio made it a two-score game. The Blue Jays defense remained stout, not allowing any kind of positive field position to the Diplomats as they held them to zero points through the final three quarters. Franklin & Marshall only registered 57 yards of total offense in that stretch of time, including a game ending interception to seal the victory! While the season may not have been a complete success, this was a resounding finish for a team that showed resilience, winning their final four games of the year. Women's Soccer: W (4 - 0), W (1 - 0) Ranked eleventh in the nation, the Hopkins women's soccer team entered the NCAA tournament with high hopes of post-season success. First on their schedule was unranked Rivier College in a game played at home. It didn't take Hopkins too long to get on the scoreboard as freshman forward Katie Derby put one away in the 20th minute of the contest. Rivier only managed to make one shot all day, meanwhile the Blue Jays were able to score three more goals from their 22 shots, a completely dominant display. Next up was Hamilton University on Sunday afternoon in a must-win game for the Blue Jays. While it was not the same one-sided affair as against Rivier, Hopkins came out strong, scoring a first half goal thanks to senior forward Caroline Marcus netting one in the 24th minute. Hamilton was able to stay within an arm's length of the Blue Jays, but a sensational performance from sophomore goalkeeper Ella Kruntchev saw her save five shots from the opposition. Hopkins were outshot six to zero in the second half, but the defense stayed resolute and allowed them to edge out a narrow one goal victory over the Continentals. The Blue Jays will face conference rivals Swarthmore this Saturday in the Sweet 16 of the NCAA tournament!

articles.title: Now that you don't have to be perfect: Netflix's East of Eden chooses to be good
articles.description: Having first heard about Netflix's recent adaptation of John Steinbeck's classic novel East of Eden through an event Hopkins hosted at the Bloomberg Center in DC, I had no idea what a gem was waiting for me. Adapted by Zoe Kazan, the seven-episode miniseries follows two generations of brothers in the Trask family in the United States at the turn of the twentieth century, amid the settling of California and rapid social and economic transformation. Although, I want to stress that this is an adaptation that doesn't require you to know anything about these characters. As I will mention, it does a great job of letting them present themselves to the viewer: through their actions, through what they say but mostly through what they try, and often fail, to hide. The show starts with Florence Pugh, who is also an executive producer of the series and plays our female protagonist, Cathy Ames, narrating: "I believe there are monsters in this world born from human parents." Then, Cathy drags herself through literal mud to barely reach the doorstep of the Trask brothers' farmhouse. Covered in blood and clearly beaten almost to death, she is welcomed, almost by instinct, by Adam Trask (Christopher Abbott). Meanwhile, his brother Charles (Mike Faist) remains skeptical. After all, how could an honest woman have ended up in such a degrading situation without anyone in town knowing her? To some, this might be, to keep with the biblical allegory, an Eve-bites-the-apple moment. In a sense, it is, because it is the catalyst for the continuation of the show, given that Cathy will later marry Adam and give birth to the next generation of the Trask family. But did it mean an evil change of tide? You will have to find out by giving the show a shot. Although, maybe from the title of this review, you can imagine that this is the central question, not the answer, that drives the storytelling of Zoe Kazan's East of Eden: can things be inherently good or evil? Cathy Ames, our antihero, encapsulates that beautifully by offering the viewer a plethora of nuance. It is in Florence Pugh's commendable acting (I have yet to see a transition from crying to laughing so terrifying and gripping as hers) and in the very core writing of her character. Cathy does horrible things, including, but not limited to: murdering, stealing and manipulating. And the show doesn't try to brush it off. These actions are given a carefully calculated space to exist: they don't suffocate the plot into a Machiavellian coloring of Cathy's character, nor are they the setup for a villain-origin story where we find out that "everything was for a greater, more ethical cause." She is just human. And a (very) flawed one, of course. I also quite liked how refreshing it was to see a woman in a historical drama who was given the means and empathy by her writers to show all of herself - beyond just her oppression within the misogynistic setting she lives in. Another highlight of the show was the dynamics of brotherhood. As we meet Adam and Charles in the first part of the series, and then Aron and Cal in the second, we basically meet iterations of the Cain and Abel biblical myth twice. For those unfamiliar with it, it is the first murder in the Bible, which tells the story of Adam and Eve's sons and how brotherly jealousy drove Cain to kill his own brother. That is portrayed with different subtexts in each of the Trasks' generations, and I promise the setup of these sibling dynamics is worth your attention, especially because of the color the "Cain" figures, Charles and Cal, bring to the overall East of Eden narrative. Every. Single. One. of these brothers has qualities and flaws, which I wasn't expecting given the heavy biblical subtext, in a way that makes you constantly rethink your curiosity about these characters. And in the middle of all this, we are introduced to Lee (Hoon Lee), the caregiver of Aron and Cal when they are left orphaned by their mom and dad (the latter being more of a symbolic abandonment). Similarly to the other characters, he brings about the big question: must we be good, haunted by an inherited guilt for being necessarily sinful humans, or can we be good, and follow our freedom to build our own morals and, at the end of the day, our conception of a worthy life? Lee brings that directly into his little sermons to the boys as they grow up and eventually take some weird turns, but more than that, he is such a precious character who pulls the plot away from the white-centered society we are dealing with. As an Asian American from San Francisco, we follow many of his struggles with xenophobia. In his grappling with belonging in a white elitist society or in his estrangement from his Chinese roots after being so far from home, his camouflage-like lifestyle is intriguingly heightened. And so, I have listed plenty of the show's historically relevant and poignant undertones, but I want to clarify that all of these big philosophical and cultural questions are, in the end, undertones. The show I watched, and I hope you will as well, is complex and nuanced, but it is also energetic and truly impactful. I was ecstatic about the great locations, the awesome acting, and the liveliness in the storytelling and the filming of everything in this series. There is a quote from the book that doesn't appear in the adaptation directly but that I think works beautifully to synthesize what these seven episodes are all about: "Now that you don't have to be perfect, you can be good." This show definitely embraced the flaws of its characters. Although it has some ups and downs, as every book adaptation does when choosing what to focus on, I think that, by choosing not to be the perfect book adaptation or the perfect historical depiction, it was able to be good. It was simply, but not simplistically, human.

articles.title: Canine minds: Brian Hare and experiments on the behavior of dogs
articles.description: During the COVID-19 pandemic, videos of the "What the Fluff" challenge circulated widely on social media. In these videos, owners would throw a blanket and step behind a curtain or wall, surprising their dogs when they suddenly vanished. Videos of dogs' seemingly surprised or startled reactions grew increasingly popular. Although these videos are fun and entertaining, the trend also gets at a more interesting question: what is really happening in a dog's mind? Brian Hare, a guest speaker hosted by the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences on Nov. 11, investigates this question. Hare is a professor of Evolutionary Anthropology as well as Psychology and Neuroscience at Duke University where he conducts research focused on the social and cognitive abilities of dogs. Hare has authored several books on the dog mind alongside his wife and colleague Vanessa Woods, including The Genius of Dogs (2013) and Puppy Kindergarten (2024). To investigate dog cognition, Hare's lab developed a simple experiment in which dogs watched their owners hide behind one of two large screens. The screens were then moved, allowing the owner to secretly switch hiding places. Researchers subsequently revealed that the original hiding palace was empty and observed where the dogs searched for their owners. Initially, Hare tested whether the dogs could track unfamiliar experimenters, but the animals performed no better than chance. When the researchers repeated the experiment using the owners of the dogs rather than strangers, however, many of the dogs were able to successfully locate them. Hare suggested that this experiment may suggest dogs have secondary representation, which is the ability to think about things beyond what you are directly in the present. For example, it allows you to imagine where you may have left your keys, or think about what may happen tomorrow. Prior to this experiment, there was not a lot of evidence suggesting that dogs had this ability. Now, based on the results, the motivation and cognition linked with secondary representation seem to be tied to social connection with the owner. Hare describes this phenomenon as 'their motivation to remember.' Hare continued to investigate how flexibly dogs could solve problems, particularly those involving communication with humans. In another experiment, dogs were shown a wooden block placed next to a hidden reward. When a person placed the block while the dog was present, the dogs used the block's position to locate the reward. Interestingly, even after learning the block marked the reward's location, dogs stopped using its position as an indicator when they didn't see a person place the block. "When you take the human away, [the block] is meaningless, because it's no longer communicative," Hare said. Hare then compared the cognitive abilities of dogs, chimpanzees and infant humans. Across a series of eight social and physical puzzles, dogs performed more similarly to young children than chimpanzees did when solving problems involving cooperation and communication with humans. Chimpanzees, meanwhile, performed better than the dogs on tasks involving reasoning. So, where and how did dogs develop these social abilities? To investigate the evolutionary origins of dog cognitions, Hare's team compared dog puppies with wolf puppies that were intensively raised around humans. Over seven years, members of Hare's lab raised four dozen wolf puppies, constantly exposing them to humans even more extensively than experienced by the dogs in the study. Despite their early experiences, dog puppies were approximately 30 times more likely to approach strangers than the wolves. They also made more eye contact and were better at interpreting human gestures. When it came to non-social cognitive abilities such as memory and self-control, however, wolf puppies performed just as well as dogs. Importantly, wolf puppies that were raised closely with humans remained interested in the particular people who raised them, but their attraction did not generalize to strangers. Dog puppies, on the other hand, were curious and excited when meeting unfamiliar humans. Hare proposed that the ability of dogs to communicate cooperatively with humans may have developed through domestication, the same process that gives them floppy ears and curly tails. "When you have fear replaced by attraction, new forms of cooperation are born," Hare explained. To determine whether dogs' cognitive abilities can be identified early in life and predict their future performance, Hare's team partnered with Canine Companions to conduct a longitudinal study following puppies from approximately eight to 50 weeks old. Researchers assessed their cognition and temperament while comparing different socialization approaches. Surprisingly, all that extra socializing didn't make much difference in the puppies' cognitive abilities, suggesting you might not need to worry too much about your new puppy's social life. The researchers also found that several cognitive abilities associated with successful working-dog training emerged before 60 weeks. Perhaps you picture an ape capable of learning sign language or a dolphin with an impressive memory when you think of genius animals. Across all of these experiments, however, Hare's research suggests that dogs have their own unique kind of intelligence. As Hare puts it, "The genius of dogs… is their ability to understand, cooperate, and communicate with humans."

articles.title: What to do about measles? Dr. Aaron Milstone on the current situation
articles.description: As of Nov. 14, the United States has had its measles-free status officially revoked by the Pan-American Health Organization. This marks the loss of a 26-year long streak of holding said status. Measles is a highly contagious and airborne viral disease with no standard treatment. Symptoms can include high fever, rashes, and even death. The disease is best known for affecting children, although any age can be at risk. However, the response to measles has been one of the best-known success stories for vaccinations in terms of mitigating disease spread. Two doses of MMR vaccines administered during early childhood have long served as standard procedure by doctors to confer lifetime protection on the vaccinated against the disease. Measles is thus recognised as a fully preventable disease, with the vaccine demonstrating minimal side effects for the majority of the population. The recent increase in measles incidence and even fatality across the United States is therefore a concern for healthcare professionals. In an interview with The News-Letter, Dr. Aaron Milstone, a professor of Pediatrics at Hopkins specializing in infectious disease, provided his insights into the current situation. As a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics, Milstone stressed the changes in vaccination protocols experienced by the organization. "[The American Academy of Pediatrics] now provide the vaccine schedule that many states are pointing to since the CDC's CHIP schedule has… diverted from other recommended schedules over the last two years, so that's the first time in decades where our schedules have been different. And since it's changed, I think people are now referring to some of the professional societies for vaccine recommendations instead of the CDC." Milstone attributed some of the increase in vaccine hesitancy to the confusion introduced by the Trump administration into the necessary schedules and procedures for the vaccination process. "The reason we didn't have measles in the U.S. for decades was because of the success of the vaccine program," he said. "The reason that we are having sustained spread now is because that program has faltered. So this is completely due to decay in vaccine uptake in the United States." While the current circumstances may not be entirely the result of short-term vaccine denialism when considering that several school age children are the main victims of the uptick in measles cases, Milstone nonetheless highlighted resistance to vaccination as an increasing problem. This struggle is especially concerning as no viable treatments exist for those with measles, despite some investigations into the effects of nutrients like vitamin A. Though typical precautions including staying hydrated and other forms of supportive care can be carried out, modern medicine becomes more helpless when symptoms like inflammation in the brain arise. "I think we're unfortunately going to learn more from measles now because historically… we didn't have lots of young adults getting measles infections. They had it as kids because everyone got measles. So now we're kind of at a new time where we're going to be learning more about measles in the 21st century in a country like the United States, as opposed to in a low and middle income country where we still see measles spreading." With the changing situation comes a change in the concerns of the parents who want to protect their children from diseases. Despite all of the data establishing the effectiveness and safety of the vaccine, some parents face a different problem for children too young to receive the vaccination who may still be exposed to measles during circumstances like travel. To combat these and further issues raised by the resurgence of measles, Milstone predicts a long road ahead. "It's gonna be a marathon. It's gonna be the long process of trying to increase vaccine uptake among the population. And I think what's important to note is if you look in Maryland, the rates of the vaccine in kids entering kindergarten is still very high. Those numbers don't capture kids who are homeschooled or kids who are in communities that are [more isolated]... We have to figure out how we can target resources and effort towards communities that we know have a higher proportion of under vaccinated people because that's where the [biggest] risks are right now." Despite these immense tasks and difficulties to surmount, Milstone emphasized the need for advocacy and action at every level, especially from the student body. "Hopkins is filled with students that are young and idealistic and are interested in public health. A lot of people hear about measles and think, 'oh, this isn't there's nothing I can do because I've gotten my vaccine, I am protecting my community' but I think that what all people have to start remembering is that anyone can be an advocate for vaccine education… try to listen, actively listen, and have dialog with people in their community or in other communities that are concerned about vaccines with measles, and serve as everyday ambassadors... They don't all have to be people like me. You know, the people that spread misinformation are not scientists… We need an army of people to combat misinformation about vaccines and anti-science."

articles.title: A "crude" imitation
articles.description: Children, universally, will imitate adults. It's evident in the way they talk, the way they dress and the way they play. I can still remember how, at a party my parents attended (and dragged me along to), we kids would stumble across the floor and slur our speech until it became an incomprehensible babble - an effect of us deciding that the Capri Suns in the cooler were actually bottles of 80-proof vodka. Or, how after my naive second-grade self was assigned his own textbook for the very first time, believed himself to be just like a real-life college student - I carried that textbook under my arm with a sense of pride and maturity whenever I went to turn it in, blissfully unaware of how detached my fantasies were from reality. But the one thing that was off limits for us children to imitate was swear words. It seemed bizarre - what exactly was the reason to forbid this specific set of vocabulary? Surely, then, those exclamations must carry the weight of a thousand suns if they warranted those dreaded corner timeouts, the thousand lines we'd be forced to write swearing to never swear again - or for the unluckiest children, a bar of fresh soap for you to savor. (Dove always tasted better than Ivory.) Just like many things, however, the desire to grow up proved too strong, and we would parody those banned words. "Darn!" and "Dang it!" were common cries after a rogue kickball would inevitably bounce over the playground fence and into the street. Meanwhile, "Frick" and "Fudge" were reserved for the most serious offenses, such as being the first one eliminated from gaga ball. Yet these euphemisms never seemed good enough to me. They were too clunky; they gummed up one's throat, stopping you from wailing your most visceral emotions fluidly. I pondered this question for a day on the recess field. "Frick," I thought. "Frick, frick, frick." The "ric" sound snagged on my tongue. No good. I needed something smoother, something that could carry the full weight of my frustration. "Fuck." It was perfect. Now there was a word that could do it all - you could exclaim it in joy, or you could howl it in agony - and there would be no debate on the intensity of your emotion. Convinced that I had just revolutionized the English language, I wasted no time using it; judging by the wide-eyed looks on my first-grade classmates, I had clearly made a term so stunning that you couldn't not revere it. That lasted about five minutes before a classmate of mine pulled me to the side and told me that what I was saying was the actual F-word. Thinking back now, I definitely didn't make that word up myself. Although I grew up in a Chinese-speaking household, I must've heard that word somewhere before, possibly screamed by a hurried businessman sprinting to work or whispered by the old lady looking for her wallet in the checkout line, and I subsequently absorbed it into my vocabulary. It was something that I had picked up unconsciously, unaware that it had made its way into my life. That story always comes to mind whenever I think about my own identity. I say "y'all" all the time because my elementary school teachers would do so. I brush my teeth with one arm propped up against the sink because that's what I watched my dad do as a kid. And those are only the influences I'm aware of. Whose vowels are rolled into mine when I speak? Which one of my friends' gaits do I mimic when I walk? Did a passerby, in the fleeting moments that our paths crossed, imprint some habit onto me that I've adopted ever since? If all my actions, if all my movements are influenced by other people, then what aspect of me is truly my own? Am I just a crude imitation of the people who surround me, like an AI model trying to mimic a human? But, I argue, does it matter? After all, Van Gogh did not invent the colors he used to paint The Starry Night, nor was Für Elise played on an instrument invented by Beethoven. Yet we recognize these works as distinctly their own - not because the individual components of their works are original, but because of the way they are brought together. Our ability to merge our experiences into something distinctly our own is what defines our individuality. We will never be fully unique - Picasso's art will always bear traces of Cézanne, and Kendrick Lamar's songs will always echo Tupac - but that is not necessarily a bad thing. I find solace, even pride, in knowing that everything I do, everything I think, is shaped by the people I've met. I am a vessel for them - I carry pieces of them into places they'll never visit, into conversations they'll never have and into the lives of people they'll never meet. I am, in a way, a tribute to them for the world to see. Daniel Wu is a freshman from Houston, Texas majoring in Molecular and Cellular Biology.

articles.title: How to Check KVM Is Enabled on Raspberry Pi 5 (/dev/kvm, lsmod, dmesg)
articles.description: Part 1 of this series explained how virtualization works, from the processor up to QEMU and libvirt. Part 2 is hands-on: it sets up the host and builds a first VM. The output in Part 2 was captured on home1, an SD card for my Raspberry Pi 5 (8 GB), running Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm with Linux kernel 6.12, 64-bit. Before installing anything, it is worth confirming that the host can actually run accelerated VMs. It takes three commands, and the second one returns nothing on a Raspberry Pi, in a way that looks alarming and is not. Doing this first takes two minutes. Installing the whole virtualization stack and then discovering that acceleration was never available is a much worse way round. What each check proves Each command checks a different layer, and each layer only exists if the one below it worked: Check 1: does /dev/kvm exist? home1@home1:~ $ ls -l /dev/kvm crw-rw----+ 1 root kvm 10, 232 Jun 11 15:08 /dev/kvm This is the most important check. As post 1.2 explained, KVM only starts if the processor's virtualization extension is present and usable, and when it starts, it creates this file. So the file existing proves the whole chain worked: the processor has the feature, the kernel found it and switched it on, and the interface QEMU will use is in place. Three details in that line are worth reading: Detail What it means The leading c A character device: a stream of bytes, rather than a disk or an ordinary file. QEMU opens it, and then controls it with ioctl calls, as post 1.5 described. root kvm Owned by root, but belonging to the kvm group. That is what lets an ordinary user use it, by joining the group, without sudo. The next post does that. The trailing + An ACL, an extra permission rule, is set on the file. Raspberry Pi OS adds one by default, so access is usually more generous than the basic permissions suggest. If instead you get No such file or directory, KVM did not start. On a Raspberry Pi 5, the usual cause is a 32-bit operating system: uname -m must report aarch64. On x86 computers, the usual cause is virtualization being switched off in the firmware settings. Check 2: is the kvm module loaded? home1@home1:~ $ lsmod | grep kvm Nothing at all. This is where many people decide something is broken. Most KVM guides tell you to check lsmod, and they all show output. On a Raspberry Pi you get nothing, while /dev/kvm is clearly there, and the two seem to contradict each other. They do not, and the explanation is worth knowing, because it applies well beyond KVM. Built in, or loaded? A part of the Linux kernel can be included in one of two ways: A loadable module Built into the kernel How it is included Compiled separately, and loaded while the system runs, with modprobe Compiled into the kernel file itself When it is present From when it is loaded From the moment the kernel starts Listed by lsmod Yes No: there is no separate module to list Most distributions build most drivers as modules, because it is flexible. Raspberry Pi OS builds KVM into the kernel. lsmod only lists loadable modules. Code built into the kernel never appears, because there is no module. So an empty lsmod | grep kvm does not mean KVM is missing. It means KVM is not a module. The capability is the same either way; only the packaging differs. The usual way to confirm this is the kernel's build settings, which many kernels make available in /proc/config.gz. On the Pi, that has a catch of its own: home1@home1:~ $ zcat /proc/config.gz 2>/dev/null | grep -i kvm gzip: /proc/config.gz: No such file or directory The first two commands printed nothing, because 2>/dev/null hides error messages. Without it, the reason appears: the file does not exist. On kernels that provide it, it would show CONFIG_KVM=y for built in, or CONFIG_KVM=m for a module. Raspberry Pi OS's kernel does not provide it by default, so another route is needed. Check 3: what did the kernel say when it started? home1@home1:~ $ dmesg 2>/dev/null | grep -i kvm [ 0.046684] kvm [1]: nv: 554 coarse grained trap handlers [ 0.046799] kvm [1]: IPA Size Limit: 40 bits [ 0.046811] kvm [1]: GICV region size/alignment is unsafe, using trapping (reduced performance) [ 0.046835] kvm [1]: vgic interrupt IRQ9 [ 0.046846] kvm [1]: VHE mode initialized successfully This settles it. KVM printed these messages as the kernel started, 0.046 seconds after power-on, before any programs were running. That timing is itself the clue: this is code built into the kernel, running during start-up, not a module loaded later. VHE mode initialized successfully is the line that matters. As post 1.2 explained, it means KVM found the virtualization extension and is running in the efficient arrangement where the host's kernel itself runs at EL2, the processor's virtualization level. So KVM is not just working, it is working in its best mode. The other lines are details of how KVM was set up: IPA Size Limit: 40 bits means a guest's physical memory addresses can use up to 40 bits: up to 1 TiB of address space, far more than any VM on this Pi will need. GICV region size/alignment is unsafe, using trapping (reduced performance) is specific to this hardware, and not a problem. Part of the ARM interrupt controller cannot be mapped straight through to guests on this board, so KVM catches the guests' accesses to it and handles them itself, inside the kernel. In the terms of post 1.5, that means extra VM exits, but quick ones, handled without involving QEMU. It does not affect whether acceleration works. dmesg may need sudo on some systems. The verdict Check Result Meaning /dev/kvm exists KVM started, and its interface is in place crw-rw----+ ... root kvm As expected A character device, the kvm group, and an ACL `lsmod \ grep kvm` Nothing dmesg Running at EL2, in its efficient mode Three commands, one apparent contradiction, one clean explanation. This host can run accelerated ARM64 guests. One consequence of KVM being built in removes a check other guides use. A loadable module shows a count in lsmod of how many things are using it, and a common demonstration is to start a VM and watch that number rise as QEMU opens /dev/kvm. With KVM built in, there is no module line and no count. To confirm a running VM really uses KVM, look elsewhere: at in its XML, as post 3.4 does, or at -accel kvm in the QEMU command, as post 3.9 does. What this does not prove /dev/kvm existing proves the kernel's side is sound. It does not prove that the programs on top are installed, that libvirt is running, that your user is allowed to use them, or that a virtual network exists. Those are separate checks, and libvirt comes with a tool that runs them all at once, virt-host-validate. It is not available yet, because it comes with libvirt. That is the next post, along with what each of the nine packages in the stack does. Summary ls -l /dev/kvm is the main check. The file only exists if KVM started on a processor with a working virtualization extension. The leading c means a character device, root kvm is why the kvm group matters, and a trailing + means an ACL is set. lsmod | grep kvm shows nothing on Raspberry Pi OS, because KVM is built into the kernel, not a loadable module. lsmod only lists modules. /proc/config.gz would normally show which, but Raspberry Pi OS's kernel does not provide it. dmesg | grep -i kvm shows KVM starting with the kernel. VHE mode initialized successfully confirms the efficient EL2 mode. The GICV ... reduced performance line is specific to this board: some interrupt controller accesses are handled by KVM in the kernel, which costs quick VM exits, not acceleration. Because KVM is built in, lsmod cannot show whether a VM is using it. Check the VM's XML or its QEMU command instead.

articles.title: DVA-C03 API Gateway: throttling, caching, authorizers and the error codes the exam loves
articles.description: Amazon API Gateway is one of those services that shows up in almost every domain of the AWS Certified Developer Associate exam (DVA-C03): development, security, deployment and troubleshooting. The questions rarely ask "what is API Gateway?". They describe a symptom or a requirement and expect you to know which setting or feature fits. This guide walks through the parts that come up most, with the keywords that point to each answer. Everything here is based on the official exam page and the API Gateway developer guide. AWS changes limits and features over time, so always check the docs before your exam. 1. REST API or HTTP API? API Gateway has two main flavours for request/response APIs: HTTP API: cheaper, lower latency, simpler. Supports Lambda and HTTP integrations, JWT authorizers (for example with Amazon Cognito or any OIDC provider), Lambda authorizers and IAM authorization. REST API: more features. API keys and usage plans, response caching, request validation, AWS WAF integration, resource policies, private endpoints, and mapping templates to transform requests and responses. How to read the question: if the requirement mentions caching, usage plans per customer, API keys, request validation or WAF, the answer is a REST API. If it says lowest cost or lowest latency and needs none of those, HTTP API is usually the better fit. 2. Status codes: 429, 502, 504 and 403 Troubleshooting questions love to give you a status code and ask for the cause. 429 Too Many Requests: throttling. Either the account-level limit for the Region, a stage or method throttle you set, or a usage plan limit for that API key. Fix: raise the limit, add a usage plan, or have the client retry with exponential backoff. 502 Bad Gateway: very often a Lambda proxy integration returning a response in the wrong format. With proxy integration, your function must return an object with statusCode, headers and a string body. Returning a plain object or a non-string body gives a 502. 504 Gateway Timeout: the integration took too long. REST API integrations have a default timeout of 29 seconds. If the backend needs longer, the answer is usually to make the work asynchronous (for example, put the job on SQS or start a Step Functions execution and return right away) rather than wait. 403 Forbidden: missing or invalid authorization, a missing API key when the method requires one, or a resource policy that denies the caller. A quick memory aid: 4xx means the client side or limits, 5xx means something behind API Gateway went wrong. 3. Throttling and usage plans API Gateway throttles at several levels: an account-level limit per Region, then stage and method limits you configure, then per-client limits through usage plans. A usage plan links one or more API stages to API keys and sets a rate, a burst and an optional quota (for example, 10,000 requests per month). This is the classic answer when a question says "each customer must be limited to N requests" or "offer a free tier and a paid tier of the API". Important nuance for the exam: API keys are for identifying and metering clients, not for authentication. If the question is about securing who can call the API, look at authorizers or IAM instead. 4. Response caching REST APIs can cache responses per stage. The key facts: The default TTL is 300 seconds, the maximum is 3600 seconds, and a TTL of 0 turns caching off. You can choose which parameters (headers, query strings, path) are part of the cache key. If two users get each other's data, the cache key is probably missing a parameter. A client can ask to skip the cache with the header Cache-Control: max-age=0, but only if it is allowed to invalidate the cache. You can require authorization for this so random clients cannot flush your cache. How to read the question: "reduce the number of calls to the backend" or "improve latency for repeated identical requests" points to stage caching. "Users see stale data after an update" points to a lower TTL or cache invalidation. 5. Authorizers: IAM, Cognito, JWT or Lambda? This is one of the most tested areas. IAM authorization: callers sign requests with Signature Version 4. Best for AWS services, internal tools and other AWS accounts. Cognito user pool authorizer (REST API) or JWT authorizer (HTTP API): users sign in to a user pool or OIDC provider and send a token. Best for web and mobile apps with user sign-up and sign-in. Lambda authorizer: your own function decides. Use it for custom tokens, third-party identity providers that are not OIDC, or decisions based on headers, query strings or the source IP. There are two types: TOKEN (looks at a single header such as a bearer token) and REQUEST (can look at headers, query strings, stage variables and context). Lambda authorizer results can be cached (by default for 300 seconds). If a question says "the authorizer function is invoked on every request and costs too much", enable or increase authorizer caching. If it says "a user still has access after their permissions were removed", the cached policy is the likely cause. 6. Stages, stage variables and canary releases A deployment is a snapshot of your API, and a stage (dev, test, prod) is where a deployment is published. Stage variables act like environment variables for a stage. A common pattern is pointing each stage at a different Lambda alias, for example ${stageVariables.lambdaAlias}. Remember that API Gateway needs permission to invoke each alias. Canary release on a REST API stage sends a percentage of traffic to a new deployment. That is the API Gateway answer when a question asks for gradual rollout at the API level. If the question is about the Lambda function itself, weighted aliases or CodeDeploy traffic shifting are the more common answers. 7. CORS: the proxy integration trap If a browser app on another domain calls your API and gets a CORS error: Enable CORS on the API so the OPTIONS preflight request returns the right headers. With Lambda proxy integration, API Gateway passes the response straight through, so your function must return the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header itself. Enabling CORS in the console alone is not enough. This detail shows up in exam questions more than you would expect. 8. A quick decision checklist Before you look at the answer options, find the one constraint in the question: Is it about cost/latency with simple needs? → HTTP API. Is it about per-customer limits? → Usage plan with API keys. Is it about repeated identical reads? → Stage caching. Is it about who can call the API? → IAM, Cognito/JWT, or a Lambda authorizer. Is there a status code? → 429 throttling, 502 bad proxy response, 504 timeout, 403 auth or policy. Is it about safe rollout? → Stage canary, or Lambda alias traffic shifting. How to practice this Reading is not enough for API Gateway. Build a small API in your own account: a Lambda proxy integration, a usage plan with an API key, a Cognito authorizer, and a stage with caching turned on. Then break it on purpose: return a body that is not a string, add a sleep longer than the timeout, call it without the key. Seeing the 502, 504 and 403 yourself makes these questions much easier. After that, timed practice questions help you get used to how the scenarios are worded. Disclosure: I am the author of a set of DVA-C03 practice exams on Udemy: 6 full exams (390 questions) that follow the C03 domain weights, with an explanation and an AWS docs link for every answer. If you want timed practice on topics like the ones above, the current price is $34.99 with this link: AWS Developer Associate DVA-C03 – 6 Practice Exams. Not affiliated with AWS. Parts of this article were drafted with AI assistance and reviewed against the AWS documentation.

articles.title: AIF-C01: ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore or LLM-as-a-judge? Evaluating foundation models the way the exam asks
articles.description: Domain 3 of the AWS Certified AI Practitioner exam (AIF-C01), "Applications of Foundation Models", is 28% of the scored content. One of its task statements is all about evaluation: how do you know a foundation model (FM) is actually good enough? The exam guide names the tools explicitly, so they are worth learning properly. Three ways to evaluate Automatic metrics on a dataset: fast, cheap, repeatable. You compare model output to reference answers. Human-in-the-loop evaluation: people rate the outputs. Slower and more expensive, but the only way to judge things like tone, brand voice or helpfulness. LLM-as-a-judge: another model scores the outputs against criteria you define. Scales better than humans for subjective quality. Benchmark datasets sit under the first option: standard, public datasets that let you compare models on the same questions. The metrics, matched to the task Metric Think of it as Typical task ROUGE How much of the reference text the output recalls (word overlap) Summarization BLEU How precisely the output matches reference wording Machine translation BERTScore Semantic similarity using embeddings, so synonyms still count Summarization, paraphrasing F1 / accuracy Correct answers vs. expected answers Question answering, classification A quick memory hook: ROUGE = Recall-Oriented, it is in the name (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation). BLEU = Bilingual, Bilingual Evaluation Understudy, so translation. What Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation does Bedrock can run automatic evaluation jobs with built-in datasets. Per task type it measures accuracy, robustness and toxicity. For example: Text summarization: accuracy is computed with BERTScore. Question and answer: accuracy is computed with NLP-F1. Text classification: accuracy is classification accuracy. General text generation: accuracy, robustness and toxicity (for example with the RealToxicityPrompts dataset for toxicity). Robustness checks how much the score changes when the prompt is slightly perturbed. Toxicity checks for harmful content. Bedrock also supports evaluations with human workers, for criteria a metric can't capture. Trap 1: a good metric is not a good business result The exam guide also lists business alignment metrics: task completion rate, user satisfaction, cost per interaction, productivity and user engagement. If a question asks whether the model "meets business objectives", the answer is one of these, not ROUGE. Trap 2: human evaluation is not always the "best" answer When the scenario says "subjective", "brand style" or "friendliness", humans (or LLM-as-a-judge) fit. When it says "quickly compare several models at low cost", automatic evaluation with a benchmark dataset is what AWS wants. Trap 3: evaluate the application, not only the model A RAG chatbot or an agent can fail even with a strong model: wrong documents retrieved, a tool call that fails, a workflow that stops halfway. The exam guide explicitly mentions evaluating applications built on FMs, such as RAG, agents and workflows. A sample question A company wants to compare three foundation models for summarizing customer support tickets. It needs a quick, low-cost comparison that measures how well each summary preserves the meaning of a reference summary, even when different words are used. Which approach fits best? A. Run a human evaluation job with a private workforce B. Use automatic evaluation with BERTScore C. Measure BLEU against a translated reference D. Track cost per interaction in production Answer: B. Quick and low-cost points to automatic evaluation. "Preserves the meaning, even with different words" points to BERTScore, which uses semantic similarity instead of exact word overlap. BLEU is word-precision based and typical for translation; cost per interaction is a business metric, not a quality metric. Checklist before exam day ROUGE → summarization (recall), BLEU → translation (precision), BERTScore → meaning. Subjective quality → human evaluation or LLM-as-a-judge. Business questions → completion rate, satisfaction, cost per interaction. Read the official AIF-C01 exam guide for the full task statements. I wrote 6 AIF-C01 practice exams with an explanation for every option. Until November 28 it's $34.99 with this link: https://www.udemy.com/course/aws-ai-practitioner-aif-c01-6-practice-exams/?couponCode=AIFC01LAUNCH. Not affiliated with or endorsed by AWS.

articles.title: Everything you always wanted to know about Secure Exclaves but were afraid to ask
articles.description: We were first publicly introduced to Secure Exclaves when Apple introduced Siri Recap with watchOS 26. Now a recently published Apple security research paper sees them discussed as a protection for person recognition in HomeView. They are part of a new security architecture designed to protect user privacy even while computing becomes more ambient, smarter, and more pervasive. While it’s good that Apple is thinking about such things, there is no guarantee at all that other companies, or even governments, will take steps to protect people’s privacy as what are effectively surveillance technologies go mainstream. So, what are Secure Exclaves? Secure Exclaves are compartmentalized runtimes that make up a new security architecture in Apple silicon. The system uses an Apple-customized L4 microkernel, originally built for deployments like the Secure Enclave Processor. This provides a highly isolated environment in which to process camera and microphone data in such a way that only specific metadata is shared with the main operating system. The idea behind this is that this information is not stored, shared, or digitized in the conventional sense, even while the data itself can be processed. All that is stored is the condensed text and summary. One way to think about this is that even if you end up with a summarized note concerning the meeting, the raw data of the meeting itself is never stored, which means — Apple claims — it can’t be accessed by your devices, Apple, or anyone else. (Though the summary text that is created can be accessed.) Overall, it’s an architecture that lets AI work with data on the fly, working only with the real-life data stream most of the time. There are two primary modes for the tech: ambient and active. When in ambient mode, only specific information can be shared with the rest of the system. In active mode, such as a Siri conversation or a FaceTime call, data can be released to the main OS, with a secure indicator (usually a physical light) telling the user. When it comes to HomeView person recognition, only metadata such as a person identifier, position, and confidence level ever gets to the OS, Apple said. Why Secure Exclaves? We live in a digital reality in which high profile people can expect to be attacked digitally. We exist in a realm in which human rights defenders, intellectuals, artists, and business leaders are regularly targeted by out of control state-adjacent surveillance-as-a-service mercenaries. That reality underlines the inherent insecurity as our digital lives become data. Apple is well aware of that, which is why it is attempting to find some way to deliver digital convenience, but not at the cost of personal privacy. “Our goal is to keep ambient sensor data secure even against highly sophisticated attacks, while giving users a clear, reliable, and tamper-resistant signal whenever their sensors are fully active,” Apple explains. How do Secure Exclaves work? Apple has developed the system because it believes ambient sensing should never record audio or video or expose it to the rest of the operating system. To achieve this, the tech helps reduce the stream to simple signals, protects the raw data while it is being processed, and discards it after the work is done. Secure Exclaves are compartmentalized in that data processed on them cannot be accessed by the rest of the system. Apple calls this the most advanced architecture for ambient sensing in the industry. It achieves this because exclaves effectively run on their own operating system, separate from the main one. Data in the exclaves is not extractable or modifiable from the main OS, Apple’s researchers said. Memory isolation relies on the Secure Page Table Monitor (SPTM), which runs at a higher privilege level than the kernel and gives exclaves a separate view of memory. Every scrap of data shared from the exclave to the main OS is audited to ensure only the minimum metadata required for the use is shared. With person recognition on HomeView, for example, Apple’s approach means camera frames are shared with a camera exclave, while audio goes to the audio exclave. Neither shares the information with the main system; they just use it as a signal that a person is present, using the Neural Engine to figure out who they are. The impact, according to Apple, is that the system itself only knows that a person has been seen and how confidently the identity of that person has been recognized. You still have a choice Apple’s approach leaves you some choice in that you must opt in to use Siri Recap and Live Rewind. The company has also popped a kind of anti-surveillance engine inside so that the system tries to leave sensitive content out. Apple doesn’t pretend the system is perfect but says it is committed to continuing to harden the system, “fueled by AI-accelerated vulnerability research and expanded formal verification coverage. “We see Secure Exclaves as a critical step in giving our users clarity and confidence about how their Apple products respond to the world around them,” the company said. Lessons for IT When considering Apple’s system, the main thought that should occur to IT decision makers is that the lengths Apple is taking to protect this kind of information also exposes the extent to which this data can be gathered and exploited. While Apple may have considered security around the realization of these tools, not every manufacturer has, and this very likely means enterprise users will have to revisit their policies governing device use in meetings to prevent smart devices becoming tools for data escape. That’s good news for manufacturers of lead-lined boxes to put personal devices inside in protected areas, but probably not such good news for everyone else. Now please subscribe to my daily, human-curated Apple-related news headline feed at The Core, or follow me on BlueSky, LinkedIn, or Mastodon.

articles.title: AI Shopping Bots Buy The Wrong Thing, WeFetch Says Barcodes Fix It
articles.description: WeFetch AI Corp., formerly GreenCore Solutions Corp., has completed its name change as it pitches a barcode check that stops AI shopping agents from buying the wrong product. Key Takeaways The Registrar of Companies for British Columbia issued the Certificate of Change of Name on Nov. 13, 2026 The lead product, gtinfetch.ai, answers for 84,810,515 barcodes from 376,271 makers across 3,520,471 points of sale Each check gets a signed receipt at rco.wefetch.ai that is open to public verification The full record now answers from France, Singapore and the United States The company announced that it has completed its change of name. It describes itself as an artificial intelligence (AI) shopping company. Its lead product, gtinfetch.ai, is built to remove the guesswork when an AI agent picks a product. How The Barcode Check Works The company says an AI agent picks a product in words, and the same words can match a dozen barcodes. Examples include the right brand in the wrong size, last year's pack, or a look-alike from another maker. When the agent guesses, the company says the shopper gets the wrong product, the brand loses a sale it had already won, and the retailer pays for the return. With gtinfetch.ai, an AI agent sends a barcode and gets a firm answer: verified, not verified or unknown, with the sources behind it. Signed Receipts And Three Regions The company says that when an AI agent buys for a shopper, the agent's choice leaves no record today. gtinfetch.ai gives the agent a signed receipt of the check, written at rco.wefetch.ai and open to public verification. Retailers, brands and auditors can see what was checked, when, and what the answer was. The mark is "Barcode verified". The full record now answers from France, Singapore and the United States. Every barcode also has its own free public page at gtinfetch.ai. The company says these three regions are where AI shopping starts. It cited figures from a Microsoft AI Diffusion Report for the second quarter of 2026 on consumer use of generative AI among working-age people. Region Working-age people using generative AI Singapore 64.3% France 49.6% United States 33.0% Worldwide 18.8% The company also calls them the home markets of the AI that shoppers ask. It names ChatGPT and Claude in the United States and Mistral in France. What The Company Says It Built The company describes WeFetch.ai as a barcode fetch system for AI agents. It says the system answers for 84 million products in 70 countries, with 3.5 million points of sale on its own record. Every answer is signed. The product set includes triggerfetch for brands, shopfetch for shoppers, matchfetch for AI agents and gtinfetch as the record itself. The company says it works with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Mistral, Perplexity and Muse. "Words were the first generation of AI answers. Barcodes are agentic commerce," said Matthew Keddy, Chief Executive Officer of WeFetch AI Corp. The company also cited a Gartner forecast of $2.7 trillion in AI spending in 2026. It cited a McKinsey projection that AI agents will orchestrate $3 trillion to $5 trillion in global commerce by 2030, up to $1 trillion of it in US retail. articles.title: OpenStack Horizon's exact-name zero hides the dashboard path
articles.description: OpenStack Horizon's exact-name zero hides the dashboard path OpenStack Horizon is the canonical dashboard for OpenStack. It gives tenants a web interface for provisioning and managing resources and gives administrators a management view. The browser may identify the service as "OpenStack Dashboard," a tenant name, a branded portal, or a generic login page. An exact search for "OpenStack Horizon" can therefore be less useful than the deployment path and identity flow. The 2026-11-16 count-only observation used sub_type=all, page 1, and pagesize 1. app="OpenStack Horizon" returned 0, title="OpenStack Horizon" returned 0, and http.body="OpenStack Horizon" returned 96. Those counts do not measure the number of OpenStack clouds. Query role Exact dork Observed total Application fingerprint app="OpenStack Horizon" 0 Page title title="OpenStack Horizon" HTTP body http.body="OpenStack Horizon" 96 The dashboard is an identity and authorization surface OpenStack's security guide describes the dashboard as a self-service portal backed by the Identity service. Horizon itself is a Django application, and its deployment inherits Django security practices such as allowed hosts, secure cookies, CSRF protection, and authentication configuration. The important inventory fields are the dashboard URL, Keystone endpoint, federation or local authentication method, allowed hosts, session backend, and administrator paths. A login page does not show which OpenStack services the tenant can reach or whether an administrator view is disabled. Product branding varies Horizon can be customized with site branding and deployed under a path such as /horizon/. A dashboard behind a proxy may return a generic login title. A documentation site may contain the full name without running Horizon. The 96 body results are a lead set for checking URLs, headers, login forms, and paths. The zero exact-name observations show the weakness of those two labels, not the absence of Horizon deployments. Search planning should include configuration terms, static asset paths, and the expected authentication redirects, but every query must still be validated. Separate tenant and administrator decisions Tenant actions such as creating instances or changing security groups are sensitive. Administrator actions can alter quotas, users, networks, or service configuration. A dashboard should not assume that the login page protects both planes equally. Role checks belong in the backend services as well as Horizon. Review whether federation metadata is current, whether session cookies are marked secure and HTTP-only, whether the application trusts proxy headers, and whether error pages reveal service endpoints. Test with designated accounts and a defined scope. Use the selected body observation as a route clue The body query is the only nonzero selected observation and supplies the link below. It should be treated as a candidate-discovery step. An organization can correlate those candidates with its own Keystone endpoints and dashboard hostnames, then validate the actual response. The operational lesson is that an OpenStack dashboard is identified by its role in a cloud control plane, not by a two-word title match. A zero on the exact name can coexist with a well-used dashboard. Asset records should follow the identity provider, the dashboard URL, and the services it can reach. References OpenStack Dashboard security guide OpenStack management interfaces Horizon login documentation ZoomEye count-only observation

articles.title: Italy Fines Meta €805M For Opening 20M Facebook Users' Photo Galleries
articles.description: Italy's privacy regulator fined Meta €805 million after the Facebook app on Android phones reached into about 20 million Italian users' photo galleries without their specific consent. Key Takeaways The fine of €805 million is about 0.47% of Meta's worldwide group turnover About 20 million Android users in Italy were affected by a gallery suggestions feature running since 2023 Meta has 60 days to ask for separate consent and switch the feature off by default The regulator said Meta cooperated poorly during the investigation The Garante per la protezione dei dati personali announced the penalty on Nov. 14 against Meta Platforms Ireland Limited. The case covers a Facebook feature that suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as post ideas while they scroll. How Facebook Got Into The Gallery According to the regulator, Facebook asked for gallery access through one permission that covered the whole app and several features with different purposes. That request came after a vague prompt to "enable other features", which never made clear that gallery suggestions were part of it. The feature was switched on by default. Once users granted full access, the app could read their entire photo library, generally for good. The regulator said neither users nor the authority itself could check what data was actually used. The investigation began in July 2025 after a complaint from a consumer group in Bolzano, and the authority ran its own technical tests on the app. Why Italy Acted Instead Of Ireland Meta argued that Ireland's data regulator should handle the case, since Meta's European arm is based there. The Italian authority rejected that. It acted under the Italian rule that puts a phone's contents inside a person's private sphere, which comes from the EU's ePrivacy law, and that law has no single lead regulator for companies operating across the bloc. Under that rule, any access to what is stored on a phone needs free and informed consent, whether or not the data leaves the device or anyone is harmed. What Meta Must Do Deadline Report the steps it has started 30 days Ask for separate, specific consent for gallery suggestions and keep the feature off by default 60 days Report the measures it has adopted 90 days What Made The Fine Bigger The regulator cited the number of people affected, the fact that the breach is still running for users who have not updated the app or already gave permission, an earlier 2019 measure against Meta and Meta's poor cooperation. It gave some credit for changes Meta made after the complaint but called them late, since they only reach users who update the app. If Meta misses the 60-day deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent. The AI Question Left Open The case did not look at whether gallery photos are used to train AI, and Meta denies doing so. The regulator said it may separately examine a new feature launched in 2026 that processes gallery content in the cloud. articles.title: Card testing hides inside your own decline rate
articles.description: We found card testing on a checkout by accident. A merchant's approval rate fell from 81% to 64% in two days. The first guess was an issuer problem or a routing bug. It was neither. The logs showed about 3,000 attempts an hour from a few hundred IPs. Each attempt was a $1 authorization with a different PAN, and almost all were declined. A few percent were approved, and that was the point: the attacker was checking which stolen cards were still live. The checkout endpoint had no limit on failed attempts per session, per IP, or per BIN range. It accepted anonymous POSTs and returned a clean decline code each time. We had effectively built a card validity oracle and handed it out for free. The fix was boring: Cap failed attempts per session and per device fingerprint, not just per IP. Botnets rotate IPs. Add a CAPTCHA or 3DS step after the second decline. Return the same generic message for every decline reason on the client side. Keep the real code in your logs. Alert on decline ratio per hour, not per day. A daily average hides a four-hour burst. The scheme-side cost matters too. Acquirers and card networks watch your decline ratio and can flag you for it, even if every card was stolen by someone else. Where do you put the first rate limit: at the edge, in the app, or at the gateway? Which layer has worked for you? Payneteasy handles this kind of payment flow for merchants and PSPs — see how it works.

It was occupied by an old building with one basement level and three storeys, partly extended over the years without permission. The first question was whether to keep it or to start again.
